newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rivals take to the hustings, race wide open.
newsitem.headline: French rivals take to the hustings, race wide open.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Socialist challenger Lionel Jospin crossed swords on Europe and crime on Thursday at their first campaign rallies as an opinion poll threw France's snap election race wide open.

The conservative Juppe, in Marseille at his first campaign stop, accused Jospin of jeopardising the European Union's plans by seeking a pact for the May 25-June 1 election with the Communists who are hostile to the planned single currency.

In the depressed Paris suburb of Sarcelles, Jospin unveiled his slogan for the campaign which President Jacques Chirac launched on Monday: "To all I say, and it will be our slogan...in this campaign, let us change the future!."
He disputed official figures showing crime was down. "The truth is that crime is worsening and the government has done nothing about it," he said.
An IPSOS poll for the weekly Le Point predicted that the centre-right government would be returned with only a wafer-thin parliamentary majority.
It said the ruling coalition would win 292 seats in the 577-member National Assembly, with the opposition Socialists taking 256, the Communists 28 and the far-right National Front one.
Thirty-one percent of those questioned on Tuesday and Wednesday did not state their voting intention.
Juppe's office confirmed that ministers had been told to hold 1998 state spending unchanged in nominal terms for the second successive year, meaning a cut of more than one percent in real terms.
But it sought to offset the impression of austerity by trumpeting signs of an economic upturn ahead of the election, likely to be dominated by the issues of unemployment, taxes and purchasing power.

"Growth is taking off again," Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said, pointing to what he called robust industrial production figures. He said France might make more tax cuts than planned if economic growth exceeded forecasts for 1997.

A Louis Harris survey for Valeurs Actuelles magazine said most voters believed there were alternatives to the government's economic policies meant to prepare for the single European currency from 1999.

And 69 percent of those quizzed favoured a new referendum on the introduction of the euro currency. Voters narrowly approved the Maastricht treaty on European union, including the currency, in a 1992 referendum.
The Harris survey, taken before Chirac announced the election, said 50 percent thought the single currency would fail to help "a return to economic growth", while 43 percent felt it could succeed.
Seventy-three percent believed the euro would not help to reduce unemployment in major European nations, with just 20 percent saying it would.

The Socialists, who say they favour the euro but not at the price of more austerity, accused the conservatives of trying to secure re-election before imposing draconian new measures to help to qualify for the single currency.
The ruling coalition partners said at a joint leadership meeting chaired by the RPR's Juppe and the UDF's Francois Leotard that their common manifesto should be ready on Monday.

Private television channel TF1 invited the leaders of the four biggest parties -- the RPR, UDF, Socialists and Communists -- to a live debate on May 20. Juppe and Jospin have already said they would welcome a face-to-face debate.
